conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal-mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, because every new mom deserves a safe space to talk about the emotional ups and downs that can come with motherhood.

We’ll use a quick screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a 10-question form that helps us see whether you might be experiencing postpartum depression or anxiety. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you over the past seven days. Everything you share stays confidential within the care team, and we’ll move at whatever pace feels comfortable.

When you’re ready, we can begin with the first question.
Good morning, Dr. Bennett. I… I guess I’m ready. I’ve just been really tired, and everything feels kind of heavy lately, but I’ll answer the best I can.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not very much… maybe once or twice this week my husband said something silly and I cracked a smile, but it felt forced. Mostly I just feel flat, like nothing’s really funny anymore, even when I know it should be.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Hardly at all. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. I still try to go through the motions, but the enjoyment part just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot of the time. If the baby spits up more than usual, I’m sure it’s because I ate something “wrong.” When she wouldn’t nap yesterday, I kept thinking it’s because I’m not doing the routine right, that a “good mom” would know how to settle her. I lie in bed replaying every little thing, convinced it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly need to check if she’s still breathing, or I’ll imagine her choking on spit-up and rush to hold her upright. There’s this constant tightness in my chest, like something bad is about to happen, even when nothing’s wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—several times this week. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get enough air. Once, I was just folding her tiny onesies and suddenly pictured her not waking up from a nap; I had to set the laundry down and go stare at her in the bassinet to convince myself she was okay. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time. It feels like I’m drowning in little tasks—bottles, diapers, trying to sleep when she sleeps but then the washer buzzes or the dog barks. I start one thing, remember three others, and end up just standing in the kitchen fighting back tears because I can’t figure out what to tackle first.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off—keeps replaying everything I might have messed up that day or running through scary “what-ifs” about the baby. Some nights I fall asleep okay, then jolt awake at 2 a.m. and can’t drift off again for an hour or more.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s me, most days. There’s this heavy sadness that just sits on me. I’ll look at my daughter and feel like I should be glowing, but instead I’m fighting tears half the time. It’s like a gray cloud that won’t lift, even when nothing specific is wrong.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times this week. Yesterday I put her in the car seat and couldn’t get the buckle to click right away—such a dumb little thing—and I just burst into tears on the porch. I felt so stupid for crying over a buckle, but I couldn’t stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself.

I hear how heavy life feels right now-how the joy you once found in little pleasures has faded and everyday tasks feel overwhelming. You describe a constant knot of worry about your baby's safety, nightly racing thoughts, and a sadness that settles over most days, leaving you in tears over a stuck buckle. Yet through this fog you are still showing up, caring for your daughter, and openly sharing your pain, which takes real courage.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports minimal smiling once or twice, describes feeling "flat" and unable to find things funny, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Hardly at all" and describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent self-blame for routine infant issues, indicating this occurs "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, physiologically-felt anxiety without external cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden episodes of intense fear/panic with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time" and unable to manage multiple tasks, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts and repeated middle-of-the-night awakenings lasting over an hour, indicating sleep problems "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, heavy sadness occurring "most days," aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying occurred "a few times this week" and describes a specific incident where she "burst into tears" and "couldn't stop," aligning with "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 25 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Items mapping to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> include: depressed mood most days (<quote>heavy sadness that just sits on me</quote>), markedly diminished interest (<quote>the enjoyment part just isn't there</quote>), guilt/worthlessness (<quote>convinced it's my fault</quote>), concentration difficulties (<quote>can't figure out what to tackle first</quote>), and insomnia. Co-occurring <sym>anxiety symptoms</sym> and panic attacks (Q4, Q5) are common in postpartum presentations. No self-harm ideation (Q10 = 0) lowers immediate safety risk but does not negate the need for urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within the next few days
2. Begin evidence-based treatment discussion-consider <med>CBT</med> and/or <med>sertraline</med>, the first-line antidepressant compatible with breastfeeding
3. Encourage 20-30 minutes of daylight walking and acceptance of help with night feeds to support sleep hygiene
4. Provide local <med>postpartum support group</med> contacts and 24/7 warmline numbers for emotional backup
5. Schedule EPDS re-screen in two weeks to monitor progress after intervention
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant age not specified)  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: [licensed mental health professional]

Presenting Concerns  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Recurrent, intrusive worries about infant safety; panic episodes with physiological arousal  
- Sleep disruption (initial insomnia, middle-of-night rumination) unrelated to infant needs  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and “drowning” in routine tasks  

Screening Findings (EPDS-10 domain equivalents)  
Affect: Sadness, flat affect, loss of enjoyment Q2, Q8, Q9  
Anhedonia: Minimal laughter/pleasure Q1  
Guilt/Self-blame: Excessive, inappropriate Q3  
Anxiety: Daily free-floating worry, panic symptoms Q4, Q5  
Coping: Frequent feeling that “things are on top of me” Q6  
Sleep: Mood-related insomnia Q7  
Self-harm: Denied Q10  

Risk Level  
Moderate–high for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; no current self-harm ideation.

Recommendations  
1. Complete Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (if not done).  
2. Prompt referral to OB/GYN or perinatal psychiatry for formal evaluation.  
3. Provide perinatal mental health resources; safety-plan education.
